items.title: Willis's 'lads'
items.claim: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) studied working-class boys in a Midlands school. What did he argue they were doing through their counter-school culture?

options.text: Actively rejecting school in ways that prepared them for manual labour

items.reveal_title: Resistance that reproduced the very inequality it opposed
items.reveal:
Willis combined Marxist theory with ethnography to argue the 'lads' partially saw through school ideology but their rejection led them into the same factory jobs their fathers held.

The study influenced both education research and cultural studies.
items.why: Ethnographic fieldwork can reveal mechanisms of class reproduction invisible in statistics.

items.title: Weber's iron cage
items.claim: Max Weber argued modernity was driven by rationalisation. What did his 'iron cage' (stahlhartes Gehause) refer to?

options.text: The bureaucratic and economic systems constraining individual freedom in modern society

items.reveal_title: Bureaucratic rationality as a constraining structure
items.reveal:
In The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), Weber argued the rational pursuit of efficiency would outlast the religious motives that birthed it, trapping moderns in a structure they could not easily escape.

Parsons's English translation 'iron cage' is now standard; 'shell as hard as steel' is closer to the German.
items.why: Translation shapes how foundational concepts travel between languages and disciplines.

items.title: Oakley's domestic labour finding
items.claim: Ann Oakley's The Sociology of Housework (1974) interviewed 40 London housewives. What did most report about housework?

options.text: It was monotonous, low-status and isolating
It was equally shared with husbands
It was paid at market rates

items.reveal:
Oakley reported 70% of respondents expressed dissatisfaction. Her work established housework as a legitimate object of sociological study.

Later 'second shift' research (Hochschild, 1989) extended the analysis to employed women.
items.why: Recognising unpaid labour as work reframed measurements of economic activity.
